prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: I keep IceCube first, and having read the full round-1 exchange I can say more precisely why. The discovery criterion asks what we learned about nature that we did not know, and the answer here is unambiguous: a flux of neutrinos at TeV to PeV energies of extraterrestrial origin, which no theory could have delivered in advance. It was extracted from a background of atmospheric muons and neutrinos that exceeds the signal by many orders of magnitude, and it was found in several analysis channels with different systematics (through-going muons, contained cascades, starting events). That is the calibration-and-systematics work that makes a result believable, and I know from my own instruments how long it takes. The citation I propose rests on the diffuse flux alone. I do not ask the committee to treat TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 or the Galactic plane as part of the prize; they show the window is productive, but they are not what makes the discovery secure. Olsson's distinction between a new observation and a better measurement, made in her reply to me, is the criterion I would apply, and by it B016 is clearly on the discovery side while B045 is on the improvement side. The result will not be overturned, and the cubic-kilometre concept that made it possible is a decisive instrument contribution.
statement.case_against: The credit is the real weakness, and round 1 did not remove it. Halzen conceived and drove the cubic-kilometre programme and Karle held central roles in construction and in the discovery-era analyses, but AMANDA-era leaders, the IceCube spokespersons and analysis leads, and the Baikal and ANTARES pioneers all have a claim to be mentioned, and I cannot settle the split from the supplied text. Danielsson is right that the source picture rests mostly on one experiment and awaits an independent check by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD. Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth are right that B045 has a cleaner credit and reproduction built into the field, and that confidence is worth weight. I do not agree that this is enough to put it first: its distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes is a real argument, and the redefinition of the second, its main consequence, has not happened. If the committee finds after checking the historical record that Halzen and Karle cannot be defended as the two decisive names, the case for B016 weakens materially and I would move to B045.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B016 with the same two names, but says the prize would be premature by some years if the source identifications must be independently confirmed first, and names B045 as the safer alternative.
responses.response: We agree that the citation must stand on the diffuse flux, and that is why I would write it that way. The diffuse flux was seen in several channels with different techniques inside one detector, and its reality does not depend on whether TXS 0506+056 turns out to be the final word on sources. Your premature-by-some-years scenario applies only if the prize is for source identification. I would make that explicit in the citation, so the question of KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD confirmation is separate. On names, I stay where we both are: neither of us can verify the full AMANDA-era record from the supplied text, and I will treat a clear contradiction of the Halzen-Karle pairing as a reason to move.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B045 for its independent reproduction in many national laboratories, 1e-18 accuracy, geodesy and tests of constants, and a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I give the independent reproduction real weight, and I agree B045 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. But the argument that comparison between clocks is built-in confirmation applies to a measurement whose result is a number and an instrument, while the claim I am testing for B016 is a discovery of a new phenomenon. The diffuse flux is also confirmed several ways, though inside one collaboration. On your own list B045's largest consequences are still prospective, and you accept that the citation overlaps neighbouring prizes. I would not block B045 and it is my first alternative, but I would not prefer it to a new observational window unless the IceCube credit proved indefensible.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B040 and argues that the HgTe experiment showed a phenomenon not seen before, whereas the lattice clock does an existing kind of measurement much better.
responses.response: That distinction is the most useful point anyone made to me in round 1, and I have adopted it. It is the same test that I apply to B016, which gives me more confidence I am not just favouring detectors. Where I differ is on maturity and credit for B040: you and Eriksson still disagree over Mele versus Hasan, and the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal with Zhang deceased is a real gap that three names cannot cover. I would rank B040 above the quantum-technology ballots and ahead of B038, but the credit problem there looks no easier to resolve than mine, and the 2016 prize makes distinctness a live question.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B045 and says she would want to hear from both Danielsson and me whether Halzen and Karle capture the decisive contributions before she could support B016 over it.
responses.response: I take the request seriously. My answer is that Halzen drove the concept and the funding of the cubic-kilometre detector, and Karle was a leader of the construction and the discovery analyses, so a pair is defensible. It is not unambiguous, and I will not say it is. What I can say is that the choice for any large-collaboration prize is between a defensible pair and an indefensible one, and the Halzen-Karle pair belongs to the first kind on the record I know. If you and others find a decisive contribution that I am missing, say so now. Short of that, I see a fallback in B045 between our lists, as you note.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen and Karle are the two names with the strongest claim to the decisive contribution, given AMANDA, other IceCube leaders and analysis leads, and the deep-water programmes. I cannot resolve this from the supplied text.
Whether the committee accepts a diffuse-flux-only citation, or insists on independent confirmation of the source associations from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD first.
Whether the lattice clock (B045) is a distinct discovery or a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, which lies outside my field and which I judge only through colleagues.
Whether the committee can find a defensible three-name configuration for B040 given the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan questions, since if it can the ranking of B040 against B016 could change.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Halzen, Karle or the IceCube collaboration, and I will recuse myself from B016 if a collaboration link emerges. I work in astroparticle detectors (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), so I may have a taste bias toward detector-driven results, which I have tried to counter by testing B016 against the same independence and credit criteria I apply to others. As Chair I have summarised the committee's positions, including my own support for B016, as one of the supporters, and I do not treat support counts as a substitute for the scientific case.
